'''Hillel "Harry" Furstenberg''' ({{langx|he|הלל (הארי) פורסטנברג}}; born September 29, 1935) is a German-born American-Israeli mathematician and professor emeritus at the [[Hebrew University of Jerusalem]]. He is a member of the [[Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities]] and [[U.S. National Academy of Sciences]] and a laureate of the [[Abel Prize]] and the [[Wolf Prize in Mathematics]]. He is known for his application of [[probability theory]] and [[ergodic theory]] methods to other areas of mathematics, including [[number theory]] and [[Lie group]]s.

==Biography==
Furstenberg was born to [[German Jews]] in [[Nazi Germany]], in 1935 (originally named "Fürstenberg"). In 1939, shortly after [[Kristallnacht]], his family escaped to the United States and settled in the [[Washington Heights, Manhattan|Washington Heights]] neighborhood of New York City, escaping the [[Holocaust]].<ref>Chang, Kenneth. [https://www.nytimes.com/2020/03/18/science/abel-prize-mathematics.html "Abel Prize in Mathematics Shared by 2 Trailblazers of Probability and Dynamics Hillel Furstenberg, 84, and Gregory Margulis, 74, both retired professors, share the mathematics equivalent of a Nobel Prize."] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200318152437/https://www.nytimes.com/2020/03/18/science/abel-prize-mathematics.html |date=March 18, 2020 }}, ''[[The New York Times]]'', March 18, 2020. Accessed March 18, 2020. "Dr. Furstenberg was born in Berlin in 1935. His family, which was Jewish, was able to leave Germany just before the start of World War II and made its way to the United States, settling in New York City in the Washington Heights neighborhood in Manhattan."</ref> He attended [[Marsha Stern Talmudical Academy]] and then [[Yeshiva University]], where he concluded his BA and MSc studies at the age of 20 in 1955.<ref>{{Cite web
 |title=YU Alumnus Dr. Hillel Furstenberg Wins the Abel Prize, the “Math Nobel”
 |url=https://www.yu.edu/news/yu-alumnus-dr-hillel-furstenberg-wins-the-abel-prize-the-math-nobel
 |website=Yeshiva University
 |date=25 March 2020
 |access-date=20 July 2026
}}</ref> Furstenberg published several papers as an undergraduate, including  "''Note on one type of indeterminate form''" (1953) and "''[[Furstenberg's proof of the infinitude of primes|On the infinitude of primes]]''" (1955).  Both appeared in the ''[[American Mathematical Monthly]]'', the latter provided a topological proof of Euclid's famous theorem that there are infinitely many primes.

==Academic career==
Furstenberg pursued his doctorate at [[Princeton University]] under the supervision of [[Salomon Bochner]].  In 1958 he received his PhD for his thesis, Prediction Theory.<ref name="MacTutor">{{cite web|url=http://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Furstenberg.html|work=[[MacTutor History of Mathematics archive]]|author1=O'Connor, John J. |author2=Robertson, Edmund F. |title=Hillel Furstenberg|access-date=March 22, 2020}}</ref>

From 1959–1960, Furstenberg served as the [[C. L. E. Moore instructor]] at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]].<ref name="NYT">{{cite news|work=[[New York Times]]|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/03/18/science/abel-prize-mathematics.html|title=Abel Prize in Mathematics Shared by 2 Trailblazers of Probability and Dynamics|author=Kenneth Chang|date=March 18, 2020|access-date=March 22, 2020}}</ref>

Furstenberg got his first job as an assistant professor in 1961 at the [[University of Minnesota]]. Furstenberg was promoted to full professor at Minnesota but moved to Israel in 1965 to join at [[Einstein Institute of Mathematics|Hebrew University's Einstein Institute of Mathematics]]. He retired from Hebrew University in 2003.<ref name="Abel" /> Furstenberg serves as an Advisory Committee member of The Center for Advanced Studies in Mathematics at [[Ben Gurion University of the Negev]].<ref name="MacTutor" />

In 2003, Hebrew University and [[Ben-Gurion University]] held a joint conference to celebrate Furstenberg's retirement. The four-day Conference on Probability in Mathematics was subtitled ''Furstenfest 2003'' and included four days of lectures.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.math.bgu.ac.il/~berend/hillel-conference/index.html|title=Conference on Probability in Mathematics. Furnstenfest 2003|work=[[Ben-Gurion University]]|access-date=March 22, 2020}}</ref>

In 1993, Furstenberg won the Israel Prize and in 2007, the Wolf Prize in mathematics. He is a member of the [[Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities]] (elected 1974),<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.academy.ac.il/Index2/Entry.aspx?nodeId=809&entryId=18275|title=Prof. Hillel Furstenberg|work=[[Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities]]|access-date=March 22, 2020}}</ref> the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (international honorary member since 1995),<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.amacad.org/person/hillel-furstenberg|title=Dr Hillel Furstenberg|work=[[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]|access-date=March 22, 2020}}</ref> and the [[U.S. National Academy of Sciences]] (elected 1989).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/hillel-h-furstenberg-y8iylt/|work=[[U.S. National Academy of Sciences]]|title=Member directory:Hillel Furstenberg|access-date=March 22, 2020}}</ref>

Furstenberg has taught generations of students, including [[Alexander Lubotzky]], [[Yuval Peres]], [[Tamar Ziegler]], [[Shahar Mozes]], and [[Vitaly Bergelson]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=8122|title=Harry Furstenberg – The Mathematics Genealogy Project|website=www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu|access-date=March 19, 2020}}</ref>

==Research accomplishments==

Furstenberg gained attention at an early stage in his career for producing an innovative [[Furstenberg's proof of the infinitude of primes|topological proof of the infinitude of prime numbers]] in 1955.

In a series of articles beginning in 1963 with A ''Poisson Formula for Semi-Simple [[Lie Groups]]'', he continued to establish himself as a ground-breaking thinker.  His work showing that the behavior of random walks on a group is intricately related to the structure of the group—which led to what is now called the [[Furstenberg boundary]]—has been hugely influential in the study of lattices and Lie groups.<ref name="Abel"/>

In his 1967 paper, ''Disjointness in ergodic theory, minimal sets, and a problem in Diophantine approximation'', Furstenberg introduced the notion of 'disjointness,' a notion in ergodic systems that is analogous to coprimality for integers. The notion turned out to have applications in areas such as number theory, fractals, signal processing and electrical engineering.

In 1977, he gave an ergodic theory reformulation, and subsequently proof, of [[Szemerédi's theorem]]. This is described in his 1977 paper, ''Ergodic behavior of diagonal measures and a theorem of Szemerédi on arithmetic progressions''. Furstenberg used methods from ergodic theory to prove a celebrated result by Endre Szemerédi, which states that any subset of integers with positive upper density contains arbitrarily large arithmetic progressions. His insights then led to later important results, such as the proof by [[Ben Green (mathematician) | Ben Green]] and [[Terence Tao]] that the sequence of prime numbers includes arbitrary large arithmetic progressions.

Furstenberg proved unique ergodicity of horocycle flows on compact hyperbolic [[Riemann surface]]s in the early 1970s. The ''[[Furstenberg boundary]]'' and ''Furstenberg compactification'' of a [[locally symmetric space]] are named after him, as is the [[Furstenberg–Sárközy theorem]] in [[additive number theory]].

==Personal life==
In 1958, Furstenberg married Rochelle (née) Cohen, a journalist and literary critic. Together they have five children and sixteen grandchildren.<ref name="Abel">{{cite web|url=https://www.abelprize.no/binfil/download.php?tid=76027|title=A biography of Hillel Furstenberg|work=[[The Abel Prize]]|access-date=March 22, 2020|archive-date=June 2, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200602182715/https://www.abelprize.no/binfil/download.php?tid=76027|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Awards==
* 1977 – Rothschild Prize in Mathematics.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Rothschild Prize |url=https://www.yadhanadiv.org.il/rothschild-prize |website=[[Yad Hanadiv]] |access-date=July 19, 2020}}</ref>
* 1993 – Furstenberg received the [[Israel Prize]], for exact sciences.<ref name=prize>{{Cite web|title=Israel Prize Official Site – Recipients in 1993 (in Hebrew) |url=http://cms.education.gov.il/educationcms/units/prasisrael/tashnagtashsab/tasnag_tasnat_rikuz.htm?dictionarykey=tashnag |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141012053504/http://cms.education.gov.il/educationcms/units/prasisrael/tashnagtashsab/tasnag_tasnat_rikuz.htm?dictionarykey=tashnag |archive-date=October 12, 2014 }}</ref>
* 1993 – Furstenberg received the [[Harvey Prize]] from Technion.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://harveypz.net.technion.ac.il/harvey-prize-laureates/|work=[[Technion – Israel Institute of Technology]]|title=Prize Winners – Harvey Prize|access-date=March 22, 2020}}</ref>
* 2006/07 – He received the [[Wolf Prize in Mathematics]].<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.ams.org/notices/200705/comm-wolf-web.pdf|title=Furstenberg and Smale Receive 2006–2007 Wolf Prize|journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]]|year=2007|volume=54|issue=4|pages=631–632}}</ref>
* 2006 – He delivered the Paul Turán Memorial Lectures.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://old.renyi.hu/turanlectures_vk.html|title=Turán Memorial Lectures|access-date=September 14, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190921231854/https://old.renyi.hu/turanlectures_vk.html|archive-date=September 21, 2019|url-status=live}}</ref>
* 2020 – He received the [[Abel Prize]] with [[Gregory Margulis]] "for pioneering the use of methods from probability and dynamics in group theory, number theory and combinatorics".<ref>{{Cite news|last=Chang|first=Kenneth|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/03/18/science/abel-prize-mathematics.html|title=Abel Prize in Mathematics Shared by 2 Trailblazers of Probability and Dynamics|date=March 18, 2020|work=The New York Times|access-date=March 18, 2020|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200318111014/https://www.nytimes.com/2020/03/18/science/abel-prize-mathematics.html|archive-date=March 18, 2020|url-status=live}}</ref>
